source: KICD Environmental Activities, First Published in 2017; Revised 2024 (text layer)
status: outcomes from KICD's text, word for word; skills and prerequisites proposed, misconceptions draft, teaching pack draft; mapped on 19 Nov 2026 to the Grade 5 Maths standard (two or more prerequisites and four misconceptions per skill, practical outcomes marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric); written offline by Claude, awaiting a CBC Environmental Activities teacher's review. Rubrics from KICD, untouched.

learning_experiences: share information on personal and common items found at home,
draw, colour and display personal and common items used at home,
recite poems or sing songs on personal items,
match personal and common items at home with their uses,
observe pictures or animations of different materials used for cleaning personal and common items,
improvise cleaning materials at home or school,
manipulate a digital device to watch video clips or observe a demonstration from a resource person on cleaning personal and common items found at home,
use water sparingly to clean personal items and dry them appropriately,
practise cleaning utensils using suitable soap and soft material,
observe safety and hygiene when handling waste materials to avoid communicable diseases,
sort and dispose of waste appropriately after cleaning personal and common items.
key_inquiry_questions: How can we keep our home clean?
Why should we keep our home environment clean?
sub_strands.core_competences: Critical thinking and Problem-solving: learner enhances innovative thinking in improvising cleaning materials using locally available resources.
sub_strands.values: Responsibility: learner enhances self-drive when cleaning utensils at home.
sub_strands.pcis: Learner observes safety and hygiene when washing hands after handling waste materials to avoid communicable diseases.
sub_strands.links: The skill of sorting draws knowledge learnt in pre-number concepts in Mathematical Activities.

outcomes.text: differentiate between personal and common items used at home
identify materials used for cleaning personal and common items at home
clean personal and common items using locally available materials
advocate for a clean home environment for self and others’ well-being

skills.name: Tell personal items from common items at home and name materials used to clean them
skills.mastery: Tells personal items (toothbrush, comb, towel, underwear, handkerchief, cup for one person) from common items used by everyone (chairs, plates in the cupboard, the table, the broom, the jerrycan), says personal items are not shared, and names materials to clean them: water, soap, ash, a brush, a cloth, sand for scrubbing pots. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (ENVI.G2.RUBRIC.1.1), never as a phone question: c) clean personal and common items using locally available materials.
question_forms: which item must not be shared

prerequisites.reason: Materials for cleaning the body come before cleaning items. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Materials for cleaning the home. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a toothbrush can be shared with a brother or sister if it is rinsed.

example.question: Can you share your toothbrush with your sister?
example.correct_answer: No, a toothbrush is a personal item

misconceptions.cause: Sharing is praised at home, so sharing everything seems kind.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, if we rinse it" beside "No, a toothbrush is a personal item" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Sort items into "mine only" and "for everyone". Say: some things carry germs from one mouth to another.
misconceptions.feedback: A toothbrush is a personal item. We do not share it, even with family.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Calls an item personal because he uses it most, such as the family chair he likes.

example.question: Is the sofa at home a personal item or a common item?
example.correct_answer: Common, everyone uses it

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks "personal" means "the one I like" or "I use".
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Personal, I sit on it" beside "Common, everyone uses it" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Ask: who else uses it? If many people use it, it is common.
misconceptions.feedback: An item everyone at home uses is a common item.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks water alone is enough to clean greasy plates and dirty clothes.

example.question: What do you need to clean an oily plate?
example.correct_answer: Water and soap (or ash)

misconceptions.cause: Water makes things look wet and clean.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only water" beside "Water and soap (or ash)" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Wash one oily plate with water only and one with soap. Feel both.
misconceptions.feedback: Oily plates need water and soap or ash to get clean.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a towel is a common item because it hangs in a shared place.

example.question: Is your bathing towel a personal or common item?
example.wrong_answer: Common, it hangs where everyone bathes
example.correct_answer: Personal

misconceptions.cause: Where an item is kept decides, for the child, whose it is.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Common, it hangs where everyone bathes" beside "Personal" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Ask what the towel touches: your body. Items that touch the body are personal.
misconceptions.feedback: A bathing towel touches your body, so it is personal.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: talk about family needs and wants,
draw items that represent family wants,
observe pictures and photographs of different places where family needs are met,
draw and colour places where family needs are met,
match places or facilities within the locality where family needs are met,
sort and group pictures of goods and services into family needs and wants,
watch video clips/listen to a resource person on different family needs and wants,
draw and colour items that represent different family needs and wants,
observe pictures of different meals taken at different times of the day,
keep a daily record of meals eaten at home or school for one week,
sort and group different food items into meals and snacks,
play a game of picking out flashcards/paper cuttings/pictures that show family needs and wants.
key_inquiry_questions: How can we meet our family needs?
sub_strands.core_competences: Citizenship: learner develops awareness of the local environment when matching places or facilities within the locality where family needs are met.
sub_strands.values: Love: learner portrays a caring attitude towards peers when playing games of picking out flashcards/paper cuttings/pictures that show family needs and wants.
sub_strands.pcis: Social economic issues: learner enhances financial literacy when sorting and grouping pictures of goods and services into family needs and wants.
sub_strands.links: Family needs and wants relate to the skill of counting, sorting, and grouping in Mathematical Activities.

outcomes.text: mention differences between family needs and wants
identify places within the locality where family needs are met
classify family needs and wants for financial literacy awareness
prioritise family needs over family wants
appreciate family needs and wants within the locality

skills.name: Tell family needs from wants, classify them and put needs first
skills.mastery: Says a need is something a family cannot live well without (food, water, shelter, clothing, health care, school) and a want is nice to have (sweets, toys, a television, a new phone, soda); classifies items; and chooses needs first when there is little money. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: Basic needs of a family, from Grade 1. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Classifying items and structures as basic needs. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

skills.name: Identify places in the locality where family needs are met
skills.mastery: Matches family needs to local places: food at the market, shop or farm; water at a tap, well, river or borehole; health care at a hospital, clinic or dispensary; clothes at a market or tailor; learning at school; worship at a church or mosque; and knows one place can meet several needs. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: match a need to a place

prerequisites.reason: Knowing what a need is comes before where it is met. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Food items found in a market. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks anything he likes very much is a need.

example.question: Is a sweet a need or a want?
example.correct_answer: A want

misconceptions.cause: For a young child, wanting something strongly feels the same as needing it.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A need, I like sweets" beside "A want" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Ask: can we live well without it? Sort sweets, water, a toy and a blanket.
misconceptions.feedback: A need is something we cannot live well without. Sweets are a want.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks expensive items are needs and cheap items are wants.

example.question: Which is a need: a television or a bag of maize flour?
example.correct_answer: Maize flour

misconceptions.cause: Big prices make an item seem important.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The television, it costs more" beside "Maize flour" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Compare prices and ask which we need to eat today. Price does not decide.
misconceptions.feedback: A need is about living well, not about price. Food is a need.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Chooses a want first when there is only a little money.

example.question: Mother has 100 shillings. Should she buy soda or vegetables for supper?
example.correct_answer: Vegetables for supper

misconceptions.cause: The child picks what is most exciting now.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Soda" beside "Vegetables for supper" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Role-play shopping with play money: needs first, then a want if money is left.
misconceptions.feedback: When money is little, we buy needs first. Wants can wait.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks school is a want, not a need, because some children do not go.

example.question: Is going to school a need or a want?
example.correct_answer: A need

misconceptions.cause: The child has seen children out of school and thinks it is optional.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A want" beside "A need" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Say: every child needs to learn, it is a child's right too. Link with Child Rights.
misconceptions.feedback: Going to school is a need for every child.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks every need is met at a shop, including health care and learning.

example.question: Where does a sick child go to get treated?
example.correct_answer: A clinic or hospital

misconceptions.cause: The child has seen medicine bought at a chemist and thinks shops do everything.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A shop, to buy medicine" beside "A clinic or hospital" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Match cards: clinic and nurse, school and teacher, shop and food. A nurse checks the child first.
misconceptions.feedback: A sick child goes to a clinic or hospital to see a nurse or doctor.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher (SAFE: child-safety content, read first): a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks food comes only from shops, not from farms and gardens.

example.question: Where else can a family get sukuma wiki apart from the shop?
example.correct_answer: From their own garden or a farm

misconceptions.cause: A town child sees food only in shops.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Nowhere, only the shop" beside "From their own garden or a farm" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show a kitchen garden and a farm. Food grows first, then reaches the shop.
misconceptions.feedback: Food grows on farms and in gardens before it reaches the shop.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks each place meets only one need.

example.question: Which needs can a market meet?
example.correct_answer: Food, clothes and household items

misconceptions.cause: Matching games pair one item with one place.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only food" beside "Food, clothes and household items" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Walk through a picture of a market: food, clothes, utensils. One place, many needs.
misconceptions.feedback: One place can meet many needs. A market sells food, clothes and more.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks water comes only from a tap.

example.question: Name a place apart from a tap where families get water.
example.correct_answer: A well, borehole, river or water tank

misconceptions.cause: Many children see only taps at school.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "There is none" beside "A well, borehole, river or water tank" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show pictures of a borehole, a well, a river and a roof tank.
misconceptions.feedback: Families get water from taps, wells, boreholes, rivers and tanks.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: use video clips or pictures to find out how to keep the school environment clean,
walk around the school compound to find out dangerous places and items,
draw or write down dangerous places and items in school,
practise cleaning the school environment,
recite poems or sing songs about a clean school environment,
role play ways of giving first aid to common accidents in school (suffocation, falls, burns, cuts, choking),
make papier-mâché art of appropriate objects or models from paper waste.
key_inquiry_questions: How can you keep the school environment clean and safe?
sub_strands.core_competences: Self-efficacy: learner develops the skill of knowing the school by walking around the school compound to find out dangerous places and items.
sub_strands.values: Unity: learner enhances cooperation when cleaning the school environment in groups.
sub_strands.pcis: Social Economic Issues: learner develops disaster risk reduction when role-playing ways of giving first aid to common accidents in school.
sub_strands.links: Paper waste recycling relates to concepts of making papier-mâché in Creative Activities.

outcomes.text: name ways of keeping the school environment clean
identify common accidents at school
clean the school environment for the well-being of self and others
advocate for a clean and safe school environment

skills.name: Name ways of keeping the school environment clean
skills.mastery: Names ways of keeping the school clean: put litter in a bin or litter pit, sweep and dust classrooms, slash grass, clean toilets and flush or cover, wash hands after the toilet, pick litter in the compound, water flowers; and says clean school stops disease and is a shared duty. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (ENVI.G2.RUBRIC.1.1), never as a phone question: c) clean the school environment for the well-being of self and others.

prerequisites.reason: Cleaning activities at home come before the school. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Materials used to clean. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

skills.name: Identify common accidents at school and how to prevent them
skills.mastery: Names common accidents at school (falls from running, climbing or slippery floors, cuts from broken glass or sharp objects, burns near the kitchen, bumps from swings, being hit by a stone or ball, falling into a pit) and how to prevent them: walk in corridors, keep away from the kitchen fire, report broken glass, use play equipment one at a time, tell a teacher when hurt. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: Common accidents at home come before accidents at school. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
A clean, tidy school removes many causes of accidents. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks cleaning the school is only the job of the school workers.

example.question: Who should keep our classroom clean?
example.correct_answer: All of us, pupils and workers

misconceptions.cause: The child sees paid workers sweeping and thinks it is not his duty.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only the cleaner" beside "All of us, pupils and workers" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Make a class duty rota. Everyone keeps the class clean.
misconceptions.feedback: Keeping our school clean is everyone's job, pupils too.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a small sweet paper can be dropped on the ground because it is small.

example.question: Where should a sweet paper go?
example.wrong_answer: On the ground, it is small
example.correct_answer: In the dustbin or litter pit

misconceptions.cause: One small paper seems to make no difference.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "On the ground, it is small" beside "In the dustbin or litter pit" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Drop one paper each for the class: count how many. Small litter adds up.
misconceptions.feedback: Every piece of litter goes in the bin, even a small one.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Sweeps without sprinkling water, raising dust, and thinks that is proper cleaning.

example.question: Before sweeping a dusty floor, what should you do?
example.correct_answer: Sprinkle a little water first

misconceptions.cause: Fast sweeping looks hard-working.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Sweep quickly" beside "Sprinkle a little water first" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Sweep a dusty corner dry and wet. See the dust cloud. Dust makes us cough.
misconceptions.feedback: Sprinkle a little water before sweeping so the dust does not rise.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks hands need washing after the toilet only if they look dirty.

example.question: When must you wash your hands at school?
example.correct_answer: After visiting the toilet and before eating

misconceptions.cause: Germs cannot be seen.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only when they look dirty" beside "After visiting the toilet and before eating" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Use glitter as "germs" on hands and see how they spread. Wash with soap.
misconceptions.feedback: Always wash hands with soap after the toilet and before eating.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks accidents just happen by bad luck and cannot be prevented.

example.question: Can we prevent falls in the classroom?
example.correct_answer: Yes, by walking and keeping the floor dry and clear

misconceptions.cause: The word accident sounds like something nobody can control.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, accidents just happen" beside "Yes, by walking and keeping the floor dry and clear" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: For each accident card, ask: what could we do first so it does not happen?
misconceptions.feedback: Many accidents can be prevented. Walk, keep floors clear and report dangers.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher (SAFE: child-safety content, read first): a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a child who is hurt should hide it so as not to get into trouble.

example.question: You cut your hand on a broken window. What do you do?
example.wrong_answer: Hide it so I am not punished
example.correct_answer: Tell a teacher at once

misconceptions.cause: The child fears blame for breaking a rule.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Hide it so I am not punished" beside "Tell a teacher at once" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Say clearly: when you are hurt, always tell a teacher. You will be helped.
misconceptions.feedback: If you get hurt, tell a teacher straight away. They will help you.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher (SAFE: child-safety content, read first): a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks he should pick up broken glass himself to help.

example.question: You see broken glass on the path. What do you do?
example.wrong_answer: Pick it up with my hands
example.correct_answer: Keep others away and tell a teacher

misconceptions.cause: Helping is praised, so picking it up seems good.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Pick it up with my hands" beside "Keep others away and tell a teacher" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Role-play: stand near, warn friends, call a teacher. Adults pick up glass.
misconceptions.feedback: Do not pick broken glass. Warn others and tell a teacher.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher (SAFE: child-safety content, read first): a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks running in corridors is safe if you are careful.

example.question: Is it safe to run in the corridor?
example.correct_answer: No, walk in the corridor

misconceptions.cause: Running is fun and the child feels in control.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, if I am careful" beside "No, walk in the corridor" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show how a corner hides someone coming. Practise walking in corridors.
misconceptions.feedback: Walk in corridors. Running can make you knock into someone.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher (SAFE: child-safety content, read first): a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: find information on the meaning of colours on the Kenya national flag,
manipulate a digital device to watch videos or observe pictures with colours of the Kenya national flag,
draw and colour the national flag,
role-play the expected behaviour when raising and lowering the Kenya national flag,
listen to audio-visual clips or read print materials to identify occasions when the Kenya national anthem is sung.
key_inquiry_questions: How can you show respect for the Kenya National flag?
sub_strands.core_competences: Citizenship: learner develops active community skills when observing the expected behaviour related to the Kenya national flag and national anthem.
sub_strands.values: Patriotism: learner enhances loyalty to the nation when singing the national anthem.
sub_strands.pcis: Citizenship: learner enhances social cohesion and nationalism when singing the Kenya national anthem.
sub_strands.links: Features of the Kenya national flag relate to learning of colours in Creative Activities.

outcomes.text: identify the meaning of colours on the Kenya national flag
name events in which Kenya’s national anthem is sung
observe etiquette when raising and lowering the Kenya national flag
appreciate the importance of the national anthem

skills.name: Identify the meaning of the colours on the Kenya national flag
skills.mastery: Names the colours of the Kenya flag in order from the top (black, white, red, white, green) and their meanings: black for the people of Kenya, red for the blood shed in the struggle for independence, green for the land and natural resources, white for peace; the shield and spears for defending freedom. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: Main features seen at school, where the flag flies. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Recognising places and things by their features. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

skills.name: Name events when the national anthem is sung and the etiquette when the flag is raised or lowered
skills.mastery: Names events when the national anthem is sung (school assemblies, national holidays such as Madaraka Day, Mashujaa Day and Jamhuri Day, sports events, important government occasions) and the etiquette when the flag is raised or lowered: stop and stand still at attention, face the flag, remove caps, keep quiet or sing, never let the flag touch the ground. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: what to do when the flag is raised

prerequisites.reason: Knowing what the flag stands for gives the reason to respect it. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Behaving well and safely at school. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks red on the flag means danger because red means danger on signs.

example.question: What does red stand for on the Kenya flag?
example.correct_answer: The blood shed in the struggle for independence

misconceptions.cause: Red on signs and lights means stop or danger.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Danger" beside "The blood shed in the struggle for independence" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Tell the short story of the struggle for independence. Red remembers those who died.
misconceptions.feedback: Red on our flag remembers the blood shed to make Kenya free.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks green stands only for trees or grass.

example.question: What does green stand for on the Kenya flag?
example.correct_answer: The land and its natural resources, including farming

misconceptions.cause: Green things the child knows are leaves and grass.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Only trees" beside "The land and its natural resources, including farming" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show pictures of farms, forests and wildlife: all part of our land.
misconceptions.feedback: Green stands for our land and all its natural resources.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Puts the colours in the wrong order, often with green on top.

example.question: Which colour is at the top of the Kenya flag?
example.correct_answer: Black

misconceptions.cause: The child remembers the colours but not where each goes.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Green" beside "Black" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Colour a flag strip by strip from the top, saying "black, white, red, white, green".
misconceptions.feedback: From the top the flag is black, white, red, white, green.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the white stripes are only spaces between colours with no meaning.

example.question: What do the white stripes on our flag stand for?
example.correct_answer: Peace

misconceptions.cause: Thin white lines look like borders in drawings.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Nothing, they are gaps" beside "Peace" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Point at each white stripe and say "peace". Ask why peace is placed between the colours.
misconceptions.feedback: The white stripes stand for peace.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the national anthem is a song sung at any time, like a play song.

example.question: Is the national anthem sung while playing football at break?
example.correct_answer: No, it is sung at special occasions like assemblies and national holidays

misconceptions.cause: The child knows it as one more song learnt in school.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, any time" beside "No, it is sung at special occasions like assemblies and national holidays" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: List occasions on the board. Say: the anthem is for important moments.
misconceptions.feedback: The national anthem is sung on special occasions, like assemblies and national holidays.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks you may keep walking or playing while the flag is raised if you are far away.

example.question: The flag is being raised and you are walking to class. What do you do?
example.correct_answer: Stop, face the flag and stand still

misconceptions.cause: Being far away seems to make it not matter.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Keep walking" beside "Stop, face the flag and stand still" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Practise in the field: when the flag goes up, everyone freezes and faces it.
misconceptions.feedback: When the flag is raised, stop, face it and stand still.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the flag can be put on the ground while folding it.

example.question: Can the flag touch the ground?
example.correct_answer: No, the flag should never touch the ground

misconceptions.cause: Other cloths are spread on the ground to fold them.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, while folding it" beside "No, the flag should never touch the ground" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Fold a flag in pairs, held off the ground. Say: we show it respect.
misconceptions.feedback: The flag never touches the ground. We hold it carefully.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks caps and hats may stay on during the anthem.

example.question: What do you do with your hat when the anthem is sung?
example.correct_answer: Take it off

misconceptions.cause: The child has not noticed others removing caps.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Keep it on" beside "Take it off" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show a picture of an assembly with caps removed. Practise.
misconceptions.feedback: Take off your hat or cap during the national anthem.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: listen to age-appropriate stories involving expectations and experiences on Child Rights and Responsibilities (parental care, health care, protection from exploitation and cruelty),
listen to a resource person on Child Rights and Responsibilities in a home or school,
use multimedia resources to explore the responsibilities of children at home and in school,
work with peers to role-play responsibilities of children in school,
perform age-appropriate responsibilities at school.
key_inquiry_questions: Why are child rights and responsibilities important at home and school?
sub_strands.core_competences: Communication and Collaboration: learner develops teamwork when role-playing the responsibilities of children in school.
sub_strands.values: Social Justice: learner enhances equity when performing age-appropriate responsibilities at school.
sub_strands.pcis: Citizenship: learner enhances Child Rights awareness when sharing own expectations, experiences, duties and responsibilities at home or school.
sub_strands.links: Listening to a resource person on Child Rights and Responsibilities relates to active listening and speaking in English Language Activities.

outcomes.text: outline Child Rights and Responsibilities at home and in the school
carry out the responsibilities of a child at home and in school
appreciate Child Rights and Responsibilities for the attainment of social justice

skills.name: Outline child rights and responsibilities at home and in school
skills.mastery: Names child rights (food, shelter, clothing, education, health care, play, a name, love and care, protection from harm) and child responsibilities at home and school (obey parents and teachers, do homework, help with simple chores, keep clean, care for property, respect others), and says rights come with responsibilities. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (ENVI.G2.RUBRIC.1.1), never as a phone question: b) carry out the responsibilities of a child at home and in school.
question_forms: what is a child's responsibility here

prerequisites.reason: Basic needs, which match many child rights. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Needs such as food and school are rights of every child. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up rights and responsibilities, calling doing homework a right.

example.question: Is doing homework a right or a responsibility?
example.correct_answer: A responsibility

misconceptions.cause: Both words are new and taught together.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A right" beside "A responsibility" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: A right is what I should get; a responsibility is what I should do. Sort cards with the two words.
misconceptions.feedback: Doing homework is a responsibility. Going to school is a right.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a right means getting anything one asks for.

example.question: Is getting a new toy every week a child's right?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, I have a right to toys
example.correct_answer: No, toys are a want; rights are things like food, school and safety

misconceptions.cause: The child hears "my right" used to demand things.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, I have a right to toys" beside "No, toys are a want; rights are things like food, school and safety" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Link rights to needs: food, shelter, school, care, safety. Wants are not rights.
misconceptions.feedback: Rights are what every child needs to grow well, not everything we want.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks play is not a right because it is not work or learning.

example.question: Is play a child's right?
example.correct_answer: Yes, play is a right

misconceptions.cause: Children are often told to stop playing and work.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, play is wasting time" beside "Yes, play is a right" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Say: play helps children grow and be healthy. Show the right to play on the chart.
misconceptions.feedback: Play is a child's right. It helps us grow.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks children have only rights and no responsibilities.

example.question: Do children have responsibilities?
example.correct_answer: Yes, like obeying parents and doing homework

misconceptions.cause: Children are cared for by adults and see duties as adult things.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, only adults do" beside "Yes, like obeying parents and doing homework" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: List small responsibilities children already do. Praise them.
misconceptions.feedback: Children have responsibilities too, like obeying parents and caring for their things.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: physical features on the way to a local market,
draw and colour physical features found on the way to the local market,
model main physical features found on the way to the local market,
label and match pictures of parts of the road for the safety of self and others (vehicle use and pedestrian walkways),
manipulate digital devices to watch video clips or observe pictures of activities that take place in a market,
listen to a resource person on activities that take place in a market,
visit the nearest market to find out activities that take place,
role play buying and selling activities to recognise the interdependence and connections of people found in a market,
make a shop corner using locally available materials.
key_inquiry_questions: How can you locate your local market?
sub_strands.core_competences: Citizenship: learner recognises the interdependence and connections of people found in a market.
sub_strands.values: Integrity: learner enhances honest and fair negotiations when role-playing buying and selling.
sub_strands.pcis:
Citizenship: learner enhances acknowledgement for self and others when interacting with people found in a market.
Financial Literacy: learner develops spending skills when visiting the nearest market to find out activities that take place.
sub_strands.links: Buying and selling in a market relates to the concept of money in Mathematical Activities.

outcomes.text: identify physical features on the way to a local market
locate local market using physical features
identify activities that take place in a market
value things and people found in a market

skills.name: Identify physical features on the way to a local market and use them to locate it
skills.mastery: Names physical features on the way to a local market (hills, valleys, rivers, bridges, roads, paths, big trees, buildings such as a church, school or shops) and uses them to give or follow directions to the market (go past the bridge, turn at the big tree, the market is after the church). Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

prerequisites.reason: Main features between home and school, from Grade 1. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Drawing those features. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

skills.name: Identify activities that take place in a market
skills.mastery: Names market activities: buying and selling, bargaining over price, weighing goods, loading and transporting goods (by handcart, boda boda, lorry), displaying goods, cleaning the market, collecting market fees; and the people who do them. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception.
question_forms: which activity happens in a market

prerequisites.reason: Finding the market comes before what happens in it. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Roles of people found in a market. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses moving things (a parked lorry, a cow) as landmarks.

example.question: Which is a good feature to find the market: a bridge or a parked lorry?
example.correct_answer: A bridge

misconceptions.cause: The child names what caught his eye on the walk.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A parked lorry" beside "A bridge" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Ask: will it be there tomorrow? Good features stay in one place.
misconceptions.feedback: Use features that stay in place, like a bridge or a hill, to find your way.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Lists the right features but in the wrong order along the way.

example.question: From school you pass a river, then a church, then reach the market. What do you pass first?
example.correct_answer: The river

misconceptions.cause: The child remembers the features as a set, not as a sequence.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The church" beside "The river" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Walk a classroom path with cards in order. Then retell it in order.
misconceptions.feedback: Say the features in the order you pass them.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks only buildings count as features, not hills and rivers.

example.question: Is a hill a physical feature?
example.correct_answer: Yes, a hill is a natural physical feature

misconceptions.cause: Directions given in town use shops and buildings.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, features are buildings" beside "Yes, a hill is a natural physical feature" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Sort pictures into natural features and built features.
misconceptions.feedback: Hills, rivers and valleys are physical features too.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Gives directions without saying which way to turn.

example.question: How would you tell a visitor to find the market after the big tree?
example.correct_answer: At the big tree, turn left and walk to the market

misconceptions.cause: Young children assume the listener knows what they know.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Go to the tree" beside "At the big tree, turn left and walk to the market" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Play a directions game in class: the listener must find the place only from your words.
misconceptions.feedback: Good directions name the feature and which way to turn.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the only activity in a market is buying.

example.question: Name another activity in a market apart from buying.
example.correct_answer: Selling (bargaining, transporting goods)

misconceptions.cause: The child goes to market with a parent who buys.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "There is none" beside "Selling (bargaining, transporting goods)" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Role-play a market: some sell, some carry, some clean, some buy.
misconceptions.feedback: Many things happen in a market: selling, carrying goods, weighing and cleaning.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks prices in an open-air market are fixed like in a supermarket.

example.question: What is bargaining?
example.correct_answer: Talking with the seller to agree on a lower price

misconceptions.cause: Price tags in shops seem to be the rule everywhere.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Paying the first price" beside "Talking with the seller to agree on a lower price" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Act out a seller and a buyer agreeing a price for tomatoes.
misconceptions.feedback: In many markets the buyer and seller talk to agree a price. This is bargaining.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks goods appear in the market without anyone bringing them.

example.question: How do cabbages get to the market?
example.correct_answer: Farmers or traders carry them by cart, boda boda or lorry

misconceptions.cause: The child sees only the final stall.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "They are already there" beside "Farmers or traders carry them by cart, boda boda or lorry" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Trace a cabbage from farm to market with pictures.
misconceptions.feedback: People carry goods to the market by cart, boda boda or lorry.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks nobody cleans the market and rubbish just stays.

example.question: Who keeps the market clean?
example.correct_answer: Cleaners employed by the county, and the traders

misconceptions.cause: The child sees a busy market but not the cleaning at night.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Nobody" beside "Cleaners employed by the county, and the traders" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show a picture of market cleaners and the fees traders pay.
misconceptions.feedback: Cleaners and traders keep the market clean.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: discuss weather conditions at different times of the day,
draw weather symbols to represent different weather conditions and display them in class,
observe and record prevailing weather conditions as an outdoor activity in collaboration with peers,
make a weather record or chart using weather symbols for one week,
play relevant and educative computer games on weather conditions,
observe pictures and video clips to identify ways of responding to various weather conditions,
role play on ways of responding to various weather conditions,
use weather symbols to interpret weather conditions at different times of the day,
participate in a class contest, on narrating the previous week’s weather occurrences from a weather chart.
key_inquiry_questions: Why do we need to predict the weather?
sub_strands.core_competences: Digital Literacy: learner interacts with digital technology when playing relevant and educative games on weather conditions.
sub_strands.values:
Unity: learner develops cooperation when observing and recording prevailing weather conditions as an outdoor activity.
Integrity: learner develops honesty when observing and recording weather conditions for one week.
sub_strands.pcis:
Life Skills: learner develops effective communication skills when participating in a class contest, on narrating weather occurrences from weather chart recordings.
Learner Support Programs: learner develops career guidance skills when creating a weather record using weather symbols for one week.
sub_strands.links: Drawing weather symbols relates to the skill of drawing and colouring in Creative Activities.

outcomes.text: identify weather conditions at different times of the day
create a weather record, using weather symbols
predict weather conditions at different times of the day
develop curiosity in weather conditions experienced in the locality

skills.name: Identify and predict weather conditions at different times of the day and read weather symbols
skills.mastery: Identifies weather at different times of the day (a cool morning, sometimes misty or cloudy; a hot sunny afternoon; a cool, sometimes windy evening; rainy or cloudy days), reads weather symbols (sun, cloud, raindrops, wind lines, sun behind a cloud), and predicts from signs (dark clouds and wind mean rain may come). Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (ENVI.G2.RUBRIC.2.1, ENVI.G2.RUBRIC.2.2, ENVI.G2.RUBRIC.2.3), never as a phone question: b) create a weather record, using weather symbols.
question_forms: what is the weather in the picture

prerequisites.reason: Weather conditions in the locality, from Grade 1. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Recording weather in Grade 1. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the weather is the same all day once it is sunny in the morning.

example.question: It is sunny in the morning. Will it be sunny all day?
example.correct_answer: Not always: it can change in the afternoon

misconceptions.cause: The child notices the weather at one moment only.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, all day" beside "Not always: it can change in the afternoon" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Record the weather at 8, 12 and 3 o'clock for a week. Compare.
misconceptions.feedback: Weather can change during the day. Look again in the afternoon.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks every cloud brings rain.

example.question: There are a few white clouds. Will it rain?
example.correct_answer: Probably not: dark, heavy clouds bring rain

misconceptions.cause: Rain comes from clouds, so all clouds seem to bring it.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, clouds bring rain" beside "Probably not: dark, heavy clouds bring rain" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show pictures of light white clouds and dark rain clouds. Sort them.
misconceptions.feedback: Dark, heavy clouds often bring rain. Light white clouds usually do not.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Reads the wind symbol (curved lines) as rain or as nothing.

example.question: What does this symbol mean: curved lines blowing sideways?
example.correct_answer: Windy

misconceptions.cause: Lines are read as water falling.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Rain" beside "Windy" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Blow on a paper strip and draw what you see. Compare with the rain symbol of drops falling down.
misconceptions.feedback: Curved lines blowing sideways mean windy. Drops falling down mean rain.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks mornings are the hottest part of the day because the sun has just come out.

example.question: When is it usually hottest: morning or afternoon?
example.correct_answer: Afternoon

misconceptions.cause: The child links the sun appearing with heat.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Morning" beside "Afternoon" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Feel the ground or a wall in the morning and after lunch.
misconceptions.feedback: It is usually hottest in the afternoon. Mornings are cooler.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: walk within the school compound or visit the school neighbourhood to observe types of soil,
model soil ribbons using soil samples,
observe modelled ribbons to find out which soil sample makes smooth long ribbons,
classify types of soil depending on the length of ribbons made and size of particles,
make paper cuttings or pictures of different types of soil and create a portfolio,
model different objects using soil,
clean the working area and wash hands with soap and clean running water after handling soil.
key_inquiry_questions: How can you identify different types of soil in our environment?
sub_strands.core_competences: Learning to Learn: learner develops the skill of learning independently when modelling soil ribbons using soil samples and finding out the soil sample that makes smooth long ribbons.
sub_strands.values: Unity: learner develops cooperation skills when modelling objects with different types of soil.
sub_strands.pcis: Health Promotion issues: learner develops preventive health skills when cleaning the working area and hands with soap and clean running water after handling soil to prevent communicable diseases.
sub_strands.links: Modelling objects using soil draws knowledge from modelling techniques in Creative Activities.

outcomes.text: identify types of soil found in the locality
classify types of soil in the locality
make items from soil
appreciate different types of soil in the immediate environment

skills.name: Identify and classify the types of soil found in the locality
skills.mastery: Identifies sand, clay and loam in the locality and classifies them by the soil-ribbon test and particle size: clay makes a long smooth ribbon and has tiny particles; loam makes a short ribbon and is crumbly; sand makes no ribbon, falls apart and has big particles. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (ENVI.G2.RUBRIC.2.1, ENVI.G2.RUBRIC.2.2, ENVI.G2.RUBRIC.2.3), never as a phone question: c) make items from soil.

prerequisites.reason: Modelling objects with soil in Grade 1, where some soils held shape. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Playing with soil: feeling and handling it. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Names the soil type by colour only (red soil, black soil) and misses how it feels.

example.question: How can you tell clay from sand?
example.correct_answer: By how it feels and whether it makes a ribbon

misconceptions.cause: Soils near home are named by colour.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "By colour only" beside "By how it feels and whether it makes a ribbon" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Give two soils of the same colour that feel different. Do the ribbon test.
misconceptions.feedback: Feel the soil and roll it. Colour alone does not tell the type.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks sand makes the longest ribbon because it has the most grains.

example.question: Which soil makes the longest ribbon?
example.correct_answer: Clay

misconceptions.cause: More grains seem to make more ribbon.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Sand" beside "Clay" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Roll wet sand and wet clay. Sand breaks; clay stretches.
misconceptions.feedback: Clay makes the longest ribbon. Sand falls apart.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks clay has the biggest particles because it sticks in big lumps.

example.question: Which soil has the biggest particles?
example.wrong_answer: Clay, it is in big lumps
example.correct_answer: Sand

misconceptions.cause: Lumps are taken for particles.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Clay, it is in big lumps" beside "Sand" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Rub each soil between the fingers and look with a hand lens. Sand grains are big and seen.
misconceptions.feedback: Sand has the biggest particles. Clay particles are too tiny to see.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks there are only two types of soil: sand and mud.

example.question: Name three types of soil.
example.correct_answer: Sand, clay and loam

misconceptions.cause: Wet soil is called mud at home.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Sand and mud" beside "Sand, clay and loam" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show three samples side by side and name each. Mud is wet soil of any type.
misconceptions.feedback: The three types of soil are sand, clay and loam.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: observe pictures and photographs of different sources of light in the environment,
manipulate objects in the presence of light to form shadows,
practise switching off lights when not in use and during day time,
create light conservation messages,
make posters with simple messages on the conservation of light
type messages on the conservation of light using digital devices,
recite poems or sing songs on the conservation of light.
key_inquiry_questions: How can we conserve light in our environment?
Why should we conserve light in our environment?
sub_strands.core_competences: Communication: learner develops writing skills when making posters with simple messages on the conservation of light to create awareness.
sub_strands.values: Unity: learner develops cooperation skills when manipulating objects in the presence of light to form shadows for enjoyment.
sub_strands.pcis: Social Economic Issues: learner develops financial skills when practising switching off lights when not in use and during day time.
sub_strands.links: Posters on energy conservation relate to writing skills in English Language Activities.

outcomes.text: identify sources of light in the environment
manipulate objects in the presence of light to form shadows for enjoyment
describe a variety of ways of conserving light for a sustainable supply of light energy

skills.name: Identify sources of light and ways of conserving light
skills.mastery: Identifies sources of light: natural (the sun, stars, fire, lightning) and made by people (bulbs, torches, candles, lanterns, phone screens); knows the moon only reflects the sun's light; describes ways of conserving light: switch off lights when not in use and during the day, open windows to use daylight, use solar lamps. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (ENVI.G2.RUBRIC.2.1, ENVI.G2.RUBRIC.2.2, ENVI.G2.RUBRIC.2.3), never as a phone question: b) manipulate objects in the presence of light to form shadows for enjoyment.
question_forms: is this a source of light

prerequisites.reason: The sky by day and by night: the sun, moon and stars. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Identifying things in the immediate environment by the senses. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the moon makes its own light.

example.question: Does the moon make its own light?
example.correct_answer: No, it reflects light from the sun

misconceptions.cause: The moon looks bright like a lamp.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, it shines at night" beside "No, it reflects light from the sun" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Shine a torch on a ball in a dark room. The ball looks bright but makes no light.
misconceptions.feedback: The moon does not make its own light. It reflects light from the sun.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a mirror or shiny tin is a source of light because it shines.

example.question: Is a mirror a source of light?
example.correct_answer: No, it only reflects light

misconceptions.cause: Shiny things look bright.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, it shines" beside "No, it only reflects light" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Put a mirror in a dark box. Does it give light? Then add a torch.
misconceptions.feedback: A mirror only reflects light. It is not a source.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks lights should stay on in the day so the room is bright.

example.question: It is a sunny day. Should the classroom lights be on?
example.correct_answer: No, open the windows and use daylight

misconceptions.cause: More light seems always better.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, it is brighter" beside "No, open the windows and use daylight" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Switch the lights off and open windows. Can we still see? Say: saving electricity saves money.
misconceptions.feedback: On a sunny day, switch off the lights and use daylight.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the sun is the only source of light.

example.question: Name a source of light apart from the sun.
example.correct_answer: A bulb (a torch, a candle, fire)

misconceptions.cause: The sun is taught first as the giver of light.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "There is none" beside "A bulb (a torch, a candle, fire)" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Darken the room and light a candle and a torch.
misconceptions.feedback: There are many sources of light: the sun, bulbs, torches, candles and fire.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: explore various ways of storing water at home and school,
draw items used to store water at home and school,
practise storing water in bottles and water cans at home and school,
watch video clips, pictures and photographs on appropriate ways of storing water at home and school,
share experiences on why water is stored at home and school,

sub_strands.values:
Responsibility: learner enhances hard work skills when storing water in bottles and water cans for future use at home and school.
Social Justice: learner enhances cooperation when making visits to the neighbourhood to identify different ways of storing water.

conserve water at home and school for future use

skills.name: Identify ways of storing water and say why water must be kept safe
skills.mastery: Names ways of storing water at home and school (tanks, jerrycans, drums, clay pots, buckets with lids, bottles) and states why water must be kept safe for people and animals: covered, clean containers keep out dust, insects and germs that cause diseases such as cholera and typhoid. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (ENVI.G2.RUBRIC.3.1), never as a phone question: b) conserve water at home and school for future use.
question_forms: what happens if dirty water is drunk

prerequisites.reason: Sources of water, from Grade 1. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Uses of water at home and school. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks an open bucket stores water as well as a covered one.

example.question: Which keeps drinking water safe: an open bucket or a covered jerrycan?
example.correct_answer: A covered jerrycan

misconceptions.cause: Water poured in clean seems to stay clean.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "An open bucket" beside "A covered jerrycan" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Leave an open and a covered cup for a day. Look at dust and insects.
misconceptions.feedback: Covered containers keep water safe from dust and insects.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a jerrycan never needs washing because only water goes in it.

example.question: Should a water jerrycan be washed?
example.correct_answer: Yes, it should be washed often

misconceptions.cause: The child cannot see the slime inside.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, only water goes in" beside "Yes, it should be washed often" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Shine a torch into an old jerrycan. Show the green slime. Wash it.
misconceptions.feedback: Water containers need washing often to keep the water safe.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks animals can drink any dirty water.

example.question: Do animals need safe water too?
example.correct_answer: Yes, dirty water can make animals sick too

misconceptions.cause: Animals drink from puddles, so it seems fine for them.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, animals drink anything" beside "Yes, dirty water can make animals sick too" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Talk about cows getting sick from dirty water. Show a clean trough.
misconceptions.feedback: Animals need clean water too. Dirty water can make them sick.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Does not link dirty stored water with illness.

example.question: What can happen if you drink dirty water?
example.correct_answer: You can get sick, with diseases like cholera or typhoid

misconceptions.cause: Illness comes later and is not linked to the water.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Nothing" beside "You can get sick, with diseases like cholera or typhoid" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Tell a short story of a family who got sick from uncovered water. Link cause and effect.
misconceptions.feedback: Dirty water can make us very sick. Keep water covered and clean.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: observe pictures, photographs or watch video clips of people watering, manuring and mulching plants,
water, manure and mulch for some plants in the school compound,
observe pictures, photographs or video clips of healthy plants that have been conserved,
write plant protection messages by hand or electronic device,
recite poems or sing songs on plant protection.
key_inquiry_questions: How can you care for plants in the environment?
sub_strands.core_competences: Creativity and Imagination: learner develops originality when creating plant protection messages using own handwriting, or electronic resources.
sub_strands.values: Responsibility: learner develops self-drive skills when writing plant protection messages by hand, or electronic resources.
sub_strands.pcis: Citizenship: learner develops environmental education and climate change skills when watering, manuring, and mulching plants in the school compound.
sub_strands.links: Messages on plant protection relate to writing skills in English Language Activities.

outcomes.text: identify ways of caring for plants using locally available materials
perform plant-care activities using locally available materials
advocate for plant protection for environmental sustainability

skills.name: Identify ways of caring for plants using locally available materials
skills.mastery: Names ways of caring for plants with local materials: watering (with a can, a bottle with holes, saved water), manuring (animal dung, compost), mulching (dry grass, leaves), weeding, fencing with sticks or thorns to keep animals away, and not plucking leaves or breaking branches. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (ENVI.G2.RUBRIC.3.1), never as a phone question: b) perform plant-care activities using locally available materials.
question_forms: what this child is doing for the plant

prerequisites.reason: Activities that conserve plants, from Grade 1. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Parts of a plant: roots take in water. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks plants should be watered on the leaves, not at the roots.

example.question: Where should you pour water when watering a plant?
example.correct_answer: On the soil near the roots

misconceptions.cause: The child sees the leaves as the plant and wants them wet.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "On the leaves" beside "On the soil near the roots" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Draw the roots under the soil. Say: roots drink the water.
misconceptions.feedback: Pour water on the soil near the roots. The roots take in water.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks more water is always better, even flooding a pot.

example.question: Is it good to pour water until the pot overflows every hour?
example.correct_answer: No, too much water can rot the roots

misconceptions.cause: Water helps plants, so more seems to help more.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, plants love water" beside "No, too much water can rot the roots" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Watch a flooded seedling wilt. Water a little each morning or evening.
misconceptions.feedback: Plants need the right amount of water. Too much can kill them.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks animal dung harms plants because it is dirty.

example.question: Is cow dung good or bad for plants?
example.correct_answer: Good, it is manure that feeds plants

misconceptions.cause: Dung is called dirty at home.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Bad, it is dirty" beside "Good, it is manure that feeds plants" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Grow two bean plants, one with manure. Compare after two weeks.
misconceptions.feedback: Cow dung is manure. It feeds plants and helps them grow.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks dry grass around a plant is rubbish to be cleared away.

example.question: Why do farmers put dry grass around plants?
example.correct_answer: To keep the soil wet and stop weeds (mulching)

misconceptions.cause: A tidy, bare garden looks cared for.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "They forgot to clear it" beside "To keep the soil wet and stop weeds (mulching)" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Feel the soil under mulch and bare soil at noon.
misconceptions.feedback: Dry grass around plants is mulch. It keeps the soil wet.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

learning_experiences: observe pictures and photographs of different food items from animals,
observe and name pictures of animals that provide food,
sort and group food items from animals and display them in class,
listen to a resource person on ways of caring for animals,
discuss the importance of fair treatment of animals,
observe videos on ways of keeping an animal shelter clean,
practise feeding and cleaning animal shelter (for small domestic animal) at home or school,
wash hands with soap and water after cleaning the animal shelter,
dispose of waste appropriately after cleaning an animal shelter while observing safety.
key_inquiry_questions: Why should an animal stay in a clean place?
sub_strands.core_competences: Communication and Collaboration: learner develops speaking and listening skills when discussing the importance of fair treatment of animals in groups.
sub_strands.values: Love: learner develops empathy skills when feeding and cleaning animal shelters at home or school.
sub_strands.pcis: Social Economic Issues: learner develops animal welfare awareness when participating in cleaning animal shelters at home or school.
sub_strands.links: Matching, sorting, and grouping food items from animals draws the skills of sorting and grouping in Mathematical Activities.

outcomes.text: identify food items from animals
relate food items with respective animals
carry out activities of caring for animals in the locality
advocate for clean and secure animal shelters to reduce risks to the animals

skills.name: Identify food items from animals and relate each to the animal that gives it
skills.mastery: Names food items from animals (milk, eggs, meat, fish, honey, ghee, butter, omena) and relates each to its animal: milk from cows, goats and camels; eggs from hens, ducks and quails; meat from cattle, goats, sheep, chicken, rabbits; fish from lakes and rivers; honey from bees. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms (read aloud to the child, with pictures), and no repeated pick of the same misconception. Practical, marked by the teacher with the KICD rubric (ENVI.G2.RUBRIC.3.1), never as a phone question: c) carry out activities of caring for animals in the locality.
question_forms: which food comes from this animal
from an animal or a plant

prerequisites.reason: Domestic animals used as food, from Grade 1. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.
Food from plants and animals eaten at home. Proposed, to confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks only cows give milk.

example.question: Which other animals give milk apart from cows?
example.correct_answer: Goats and camels

misconceptions.cause: Cow's milk is the only milk most children see.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "None" beside "Goats and camels" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show pictures of goat and camel milk in northern Kenya.
misconceptions.feedback: Cows, goats and camels all give milk.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks honey comes from flowers or trees, not from an animal.

example.question: Which animal gives us honey?
example.correct_answer: Bees

misconceptions.cause: Honey is collected from hives in trees and bees use flowers.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "None, it comes from trees" beside "Bees" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show a beehive picture: bees make honey from flower nectar.
misconceptions.feedback: Bees make honey. Honey is a food from an animal.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks eggs come only from hens.

example.question: Do ducks lay eggs that people eat?
example.correct_answer: Yes

misconceptions.cause: Shop eggs are hen eggs.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, only hens" beside "Yes" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show hen, duck and quail eggs. Many birds lay eggs.
misconceptions.feedback: Hens, ducks and other birds lay eggs we can eat.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks butter and ghee come from plants because they are like oil.

example.question: Where does ghee come from?
example.correct_answer: Milk from cows or goats

misconceptions.cause: Ghee is used like cooking oil, which comes from plants.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A plant, like cooking oil" beside "Milk from cows or goats" and ask the child to choose.
misconceptions.help: Show how cream from milk is churned into butter and heated into ghee.
misconceptions.feedback: Butter and ghee are made from milk, so they come from animals.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a CBC Environmental Activities teacher: a common error of young children, not traced to a study by the author.
